doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

chapter: Sound, Kenny G and smooth jazz
title: Developing a personal sound, from the Delmonte Express to bassists today
summary: He says earlier generations insisted on a signature sound, recalls the community big band Delmonte Express, and laments generic bass sounds versus Ron Carter.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Relevant is closer. To be not just relevant but in order for it to be real for each one of these musicians, they really have to — see when I was coming up, and most generations before me, one of the main things we used to listen are the older guys. One of the things they used to tell us is look kid, if you don’t do anything with your music or your instrument, get your own sound. Get your own ability to have a signature sound. Harry Carney — his own sound. Johnny Hodges — his own sound. Duke Ellington — his own sound. Bill Evans — his own sound. You hit a couple of notes — ooh, that’s Bill Evans. Ooh, that’s Hank Jones. That’s Paul Chambers. And you know the point is that that was a really serious value and even if — I can remember when I was growing up, this is like fifties, into the sixties, you’re playing some of these smaller big bands, for some jobs, Moose Lodge, the Elks, bar mitzvahs, whatever it might be, a band that was made up of half the guys were a couple of accountants and a couple of doctors, a couple of lawyers, some high school kids, university kids, a couple of ringers, the professional guys that worked around. But this was a band that worked. In Monterey Peninsula there was a band called the Delmonte Express that used to be like that and I used to like to go and play bass with them sometimes. But when I first started playing with them I used to play French horn with them every now and then when they had some charts that needed some French horn I’d go play with them. But the point was there would always be one or two guys in the band, like a third alto player or something who would stand up, and he wouldn’t — he’d play a solo but the solo would be written out and this guy’s probably a doctor or something you know, but it’s written out and he played a solo, he’d play the same exact stuff every time we played the chart. But it didn’t matter because he stood up and took the solo that was written out. But his sound was so wonderful. That’s why we had him. That’s why you have this guy. Because he had this wonderful sound that he had taken the time to develop. He’s not Coltrane, he’s not ever going to become a professional musician. But he had this wonderful sound and it was him. That was him.

And he learned how to actually develop, get a voice, and put it out there. And that kind of voice is, it’s possible for anybody to have that voice. Anyone who is passionate about the music, whether they become a professional musician or not, and that really is instructive as to how I think the next level of jazz education needs to be — shall we say — augmented. We just need to find a way to bring personal voice up to the same level as all the other values that we’re trying to instill in the students. Because in my opinion as a professional musician is I’m working with the product of the jazz education system for the last 25 or 30 years, that’s the one thing that I’m really disappointed about. Saxophone players — it doesn’t matter. We’re not talking about instrument specific here. Because I mean I rant on my website about bass players, how they go — it’s like they’re going into a supermarket and going to a white can, and the can is marked “generic bass sound” and so they take the can home and open it up and that’s them because young guys playing with microphones — and you say I’m only going to play with the microphone, no pick- ups, no amps. So then you say okay, great, do that. So you listen to recordings, you say who is that? You can’t differentiate because they’re all — the sound that they get on the instruments are exactly the same. And then I’ll listen to Rufus Reid, Ron Carter, Buster Williams and Cecil McBee, George Mraz, you know John Patitucci, all these different guys will actually, they might play through a pick-up on a record, they might play on a stage through an amp with their own pick-up, their own bass, all the set-up, two notes, that’s Ron Carter.
Of course. Even with the so-called electronic — the personality is right there.
